desc:
The subtree sum of a node is the sum of the values of that node and of all its descendants.

Given a binary tree and an array queries of node values (each of which occurs in the tree), return an array ans where ans[i] is the subtree sum of the node whose value is queries[i].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For the tree below ([3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, -1, -1, 7, 4]) and queries = [5, 3, 6] the answer is [24, 36, 6]: node 5 owns 5 + 6 + 2 + 7 + 4 = 24, the root owns everything.

        3
      /   \
     5     1
    / \   / \
   6   2 0   8
      / \
     7   4
constraints: All node values are distinct, so a value identifies exactly one node
The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
Every query value occurs in the tree; the same value may be queried more than once
hints: Answering each query with its own traversal works, but can you compute all subtree sums together?
A node's subtree sum is its own value plus the subtree sums of its two children.

In level order, children always come after their parents. Walk the real nodes from last to first and add each node's total to its parent's total. Store totals in a dictionary from value to sum and answer the queries from it.
editorial: Compute the subtree sum of every node once, bottom-up: sum(node) = value + sum(left) + sum(right). Processing the nodes in reverse level order guarantees that both children are finished before their parent, so no recursion is needed. Then each query is a dictionary lookup (values are distinct, so a value names one node).
Total time is O(n + q). The sums are at most 1,500 × 10,000, which fits comfortably in a 32-bit integer.
